iactsim: a CUDA-accelerated Python simulation
framework for Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov
Telescopes
Davide Mollica,𝑎,∗Ciro Bigongiari,𝑏,𝑐Antonino D’Aì𝑎and Fabio Pintore𝑎
𝑎INAF, Istituto di Astrofisica Spaziale e Fisica Cosmica, Via Ugo la Malfa 153, I-90146 Palermo, Italy
𝑏INAF-Osservatorio Astronomico di Roma, Via Frascati 33, 00078 Monte Porzio Catone (Roma), Italy
𝑐ASI – Space Science Data Center, Via del Politecnico s.n.c., 00133 Roma, Italy
E-mail: davide.mollica@inaf.it
In the last decade, Graphic Processing Units (GPUs) have become a standard component of High
Performance Computing systems and are now ubiquitous in consumer-grade hardware. Their mas-
sive parallel architecture offers significantly higher computing throughput and energy efficiency
than traditional CPU-based solutions. In the context of Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Tele-
scopes (IACTs), large-scale Monte Carlo simulations of Extensive Air Showers are fundamental
for data analysis. The telescopes’ response to the Cherenkov light produced by such showers must
also be carefully simulated. The most time-consuming tasks of an IACT response simulation are
the optical ray-tracing and the camera electronics response. Although with a certain diverging
degree, both tasks can be divided into independent sub-tasks (single photon propagation and
single pixel response), making them highly suitable for GPU acceleration. In this contribution we
present iactsim: a CUDA-accelerated IACT Python simulation framework. The framework is
designed to accelerate the aforementioned computationally intensive tasks, with the additional aim
of providing a flexible and user- and developer-friendly collection of tools for IACT performance
studies. These tools are intended to facilitate and accelerate instrument design studies and data
analysis. Although the framework is still in its early development phase, we present a real-world
case study simulating the ASTRI dual-mirror optical system and its Silicon Photo-Multiplier
based Cherenkov camera. This is done to demonstrate the framework capabilities and validate its
performance.

1.
Introduction
The analysis of data from Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs) [1] heavily
relies on extensive Monte Carlo simulations. A typical workflow involves the simulation of Exten-
sive Air Showers (EAS) and the propagation of Cherenkov light through the atmosphere, usually
using CORSIKA simulation package [2]. Then, a detailed simulation of the telescope response is
performed with another software, for example using sim_telarray [3].
While EASs simulation is usually the primary bottleneck in large-scale productions, the tele-
scope response simulation can become significantly time-consuming during the instrument design
and commissioning phases of new instruments. The most computational demanding parts of these
simulations are the optical ray-tracing and the Cherenkov camera electronics simulation. Since both
parts are inherently embarrassingly parallelizable, the massively parallel architecture of Graphics
Processing Units (GPUs) offers a powerful solution for accelerating them. This not only accelerates
simulations but also enables medium-sized production runs to be performed on a local workstation
with only one or a few GPUs.
Moreover, GPU accelerated Cherenkov light propagation is foreseen for CORSIKA 8 frame-
work [4–6]. Hence, an accelerated IACT simulation framework could be extremely useful to build
fast simulation pipelines that do not need intermediate data storage (e.g. run-based simulations)
and could, for instance, facilitate the development of cloud-based simulations.
In this contribution, we present iactsim1: a CUDA-accelerated simulation framework for
IACTs.
The framework is written in Python, C++ and CUDA C++, and utilizes CuPy [7] for
GPU offloading. It is aimed to offer a fast, flexible and user/developer-friendly toolkit for IACT
performance studies.
The framework is still at an initial stage of development (alpha phase),
many planned features are still missing and it is not stable enough to be used in production code.
Nonetheless, we have implemented the required features to simulate the ASTRI optical system [8]
and its modular Silicon Photo-Multiplier (SiPM) Cherenkov camera [9]. Here we present the results
in order to demonstrate the framework capabilities and performance.
2.
iactsim
iactsim allows users to develop their own IACT telescope (or array of telescopes) simulator
by providing a set of functions and classes to define custom telescope optical systems and custom
Cherenkov cameras, to visualize simulation results, such as photon hits and signal waveforms, and
read data from CORSIKA output files. The framework main modules are the following:
• optics: optical system definition, ray-tracing and photon sources;
• electronics: camera geometry definition, pixel signal processing;
• visualization: telescope 3D geometry, matplotlib utility functions;
• iactxx: a general purpose C++ extension module.
A telescope is represented by the Python class IACT. This class manages CUDA kernel calls and
the CPU-GPU data transfer associated with the specified optical system geometry and properties.
Furthermore, it handles the data input for the Cherenkov camera simulation. It is worth noting that
any number of telescopes can be instantiated, with each IACT object representing a single telescope.

2.1 Optics
The core of the optical part of the framework are CUDA ray-tracing kernels which implement
a non-sequential ray-tracing algorithm. These kernels, although directly available to users, are
wrapped by the IACT class, which manages kernel calls, preparing and structuring data to match
the kernels arguments.
The optical system of a telescope can be built with an arbitrary number of surfaces. Each
surface is represented by a Python class that handles the surfaces properties, such as shape, type,
position (w.r.t. the telescope position), tilt angles and surface Gaussian scattering. Refractive object
can also be simulated using a surface as an interface between two materials, using the available
refractive indices or registering custom materials.
The optics module also provides a variety of light sources. These can be used, for example,
to measure the system response to a point-like source or to simulate illumination systems dedicated
to the calibration of the telescopes.
Currently, ray tracing is implemented only for cylindrical and aspherical surfaces (and spherical
and flat as special cases). Cylindrical surfaces can only be used as sensitive or opaque surfaces
to represent blocking elements of the optical system. The non-sequential nature of the ray-tracing
allows photons to be generated at any arbitrary point in space and enables the definition of relatively
complex systems. To ease the development of such systems, a VTK [10] visualizer is provided. It
can render the 3D geometry of the optical system, offering a visual feedback to verify the correct
placement and orientation of each element.
When defining an optical system, a sensitive surface must be provided (i.e. a focal surface).
Rays that do not eventually intersect this surface are discarded. If the geometrical organization
of the camera pixels is provided, photons reaching the focal surface can be traced into pixels,
recording pixel identifier and arrival time. This feature is currently only implemented for focal

2.2 Electronics
The behaviour of the camera electronics is defined in the abstract class CherenkovCamera.
This class handles the basic concepts behind Cherenkov camera signal processing. A camera is
composed of 𝑛pixels and a certain number of channels, which can be
• trigger channels, for triggers generation;
• sampling channels, to be sampled after a camera trigger;
• auxiliary, general purpose, channels.
Each channel has a specific single-PhotoElectron (pe) waveform. The signal of each channel is
computed within a specific time window with custom time resolution. By default, the time window
of trigger channels is created wide enough to contain all input photon arrival times. If a trigger
is issued, the time window of sampling and auxiliary channels are generated given a delay, with
respect to the trigger time, and a window extent. Alternatively, time windows can be predefined
and fixed.
This abstract class handles the trigger-first logic and the time-windows generation. To define
the behaviour of an actual Cherenkov camera, the implementation of the following abstract methods

is required:
• compute_signals: defines the signal generation based on photon arrival times at pixels;
• trigger_action: defines the trigger logic required to raise a camera trigger;
• sampling_action: defines the sampling logic to be performed after a camera trigger.
A derived abstract class CherenkovSiPMCamera has been implemented to serve as a base for
Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) cameras. This class implements compute_signals specifically for
SiPM, simulating, for instance, prompt cross-talk and variation in micro-cells gain within each pixel.
For each channel, signal waveforms are computed through superimposition of single-pe waveforms
at each photon arrival time. The current parallelization strategy assigns a CUDA block per pixel
per channel. The associated signal is then computed by distributing the time window among the
threads of each block. Apart from the single-pe waveform and SiPM photon-detection efficiency,
all pixel-related quantities can be configured on a per-pixel basis, including the background rate.
Regarding high-background conditions, simulation of each micro-cell recovery time is planned for
a future implementation.
With CherenkovSiPMCamera, a custom SiPM camera can be written providing a specific
trigger logic (trigger_action) and a signal sampling method (sampling_action). To facilitate
this, additional CUDA kernels are provided, for instance, kernels that simulate ideal discriminators
and ideal analog-to-digital converters.
2.3 iactxx
iactxx is a general purpose C++ extension module, based on pybind11 [11]. Currently,
is primary function is to read files written with the IACT extension of CORSIKA7. Accelerated
ray-tracing and signal processing can create I/O bottlenecks when dealing with large compressed
files. To efficiently move this data onto the GPU memory, we have developed C++ module for
parallelized reading, decompression and conversion of photon bunches from CORSIKA files into
a GPU-optimal Structure of Arrays (SoA) format. It is worth noting that the effectiveness of this
parallelization depends on the underlying storage hardware.
3.
ASTRI use case
The ASTRI [12] telescope use-case has been implemented and is distributed within the frame-
work as a comprehensive example to demonstrate the framework capabilities. The preliminary
results here presented have been obtained configuring optical system and camera following mea-
surements performed with the ASTRI-1 telescope.
The complete optical system has been implemented, including the 18 primary mirror segments,
the secondary mirror, the camera protective window, the camera body, the secondary mirror baffle
and structure masts. These last three are blocking surfaces and are described as cylindrical surfaces.
The sensitive surface is the spherical telescope focal plane.
A VTK 3D visualization of the
implemented geometry of the ASTRI telescope is shown in Figure 1.
The ASTRI Cherenkov camera has been implemented as a CherenkovSiPMCamera subclass.
The topological trigger logic has been implemented, as well as the signal sampling method based
on a peak-detection circuit. A number of CUDA kernels have been defined to perform specific

4.
Conclusions
Despite being in its early development phase, iactsim already offers the necessary tools to
simulate ASTRI dual mirror optical system and SiPM Cherenkov camera. The complete set of
ASTRI-related classes and functions allows for the easy creation of custom Python simulation
pipelines. Notably, all aspects of the telescope simulation (optics and electronics configuration) can
be changed at run-time.
We have validated the framework flexibility by simulating a variety of ASTRI calibration
procedures. The preliminary results are promising and the simulator is currently being configured
with field measurements in order to match the actual ASTRI-1 camera and optics response and

actual optical and electronic measurements such as the optical point spread function, muon detection,

In addition, we are also carrying out a performance comparison with the currently implemented
sim_telarray-based ASTRI simulator using a similar configuration [15]. Preliminary results
suggest a speed-up of two orders of magnitude, with the actual value depending on the underlying
hardware. However, we found that the reading of CORSIKA files can be a significant performance
bottleneck.
